name: Inertia
kicker: Matter’s resistance to changing motion · The property behind Newton’s First Law
dates: Formalized in Newton’s First Law of Motion, 1687
briefing: Inertia is matter’s built-in stubbornness: an object at rest stays at rest, and one in motion keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed, unless an outside force pushes or pulls on it. Isaac Newton made this his First Law of Motion, building on Galileo’s idea that a ball would roll forever on a frictionless surface. It’s also why yanking a tablecloth fast enough can leave the dishes sitting still, and why more mass always means more resistance to changing speed.

tossups.p: One nuclear fusion technique squeezes fuel inside a tiny hohlraum and relies on the fuel’s own resistance to motion, not magnets, to hold it together, in a method named for this property. A spinning object’s rotational twin of this property, nicknamed the “moment of” it, links torque to how fast a spin speeds up.
tossups.r: Because of this property, an object’s motion changes only when an unbalanced outside force acts on it. Newton’s First Law says a resting object stays at rest and a moving one keeps moving otherwise. For 10 points, name this property that makes matter resist changes in its motion.

tossups.p: Einstein’s special theory of relativity is limited to reference frames named for this property, unlike his general theory. A specialized balance used aboard spacecraft can measure an astronaut’s mass in the weightlessness of orbit by relying on this property instead of weight.
tossups.r: The more mass something has, the more of this property it has too. Described by Newton’s First Law, which says objects at rest stay at rest and objects in motion keep moving at a constant speed unless a force acts on them. For 10 points, name this tendency of matter to resist changes in its motion.

tossups.p: Galileo imagined a ball rolling along a perfectly frictionless surface, reasoning that it would then roll on forever at the exact same speed, an early insight into this property. A viewpoint that is not accelerating counts as a reference frame named for this property, one where no fictitious forces, like a sideways push felt in a turning car, ever appear.
tossups.r: Formally, with zero net outside force acting on it, an object keeps a perfectly constant velocity. Newton’s First Law is sometimes just called the law of this property. For 10 points, name this resistance that matter has to any change in its speed or direction.

tossups.p: A classic physics demonstration yanks a tablecloth out from under a full set of dishes, which this property keeps sitting in place instead of sliding off with the cloth. This property’s rotational twin, which factors in not just an object’s mass but exactly how that mass is spread out around its spin axis, is called its “moment.”
tossups.r: Objects with more mass have more of this property, which is why heavy things are harder to start, stop, or turn. For 10 points, name this property behind Newton’s First Law of Motion.

tossups.p: A sensor called an accelerometer works by detecting a tiny lag, caused by this exact property, whenever its casing suddenly changes direction. Car safety engineers design crumple zones partly to manage this property safely, slowing passengers down gradually during a crash instead of all at once.
tossups.r: This property lets a spacecraft coast through deep space for years at constant velocity with its engines shut completely off. Newton’s First Law of Motion is often called the law of this property. For 10 points, name this tendency of an object to keep doing whatever it’s already doing.

tossups.p: Unlike its rotational cousin, which is measured in kilogram-meters-squared, this property itself carries no unit of its own, since it is a tendency rather than a numeric quantity. Nuclear engineers exploit this exact property in a fusion technique that squeezes fuel inside a hohlraum instead of using magnetic fields.
tossups.r: A reference frame that isn’t accelerating is named for this property, and in such a frame no fictitious forces like the Coriolis force ever appear. For 10 points, name this property that Newton’s First Law says keeps a moving object moving and a resting object at rest.

tossups.p: French philosopher Descartes argued that a moving body naturally keeps moving in a straight line, an early step toward understanding this property, which Newton later built into his first law of motion in his 1687 book. A viewpoint that isn’t accelerating is a reference frame named for this property, where no fictitious forces appear.
tossups.r: This property is often mixed up with mass itself, even though mass is really just the numerical measure of how much of this property an object has. For 10 points, name this tendency of objects to resist a change in their motion.

tossups.p: General relativity’s equivalence principle says the mass that measures this property always equals the mass that feels gravity. A specialized balance used aboard spacecraft can measure an astronaut’s mass in the weightlessness of orbit by relying on this property instead of weight.

trap.title: Inertia, mass, or moment?
trap.body: Mass and inertia are closely linked but not identical: mass is the numerical measure of how much inertia an object has, so a question built entirely around a formula, a unit, or a numeric value usually wants “mass” instead. “Moment of inertia” is a related but distinct rotational quantity, measured in kilogram-meters-squared, and its real answer line explicitly refuses the bare word “inertia.”
trap.fix: If the clues mention torque, angular acceleration, or a shape-dependent spinning quantity, the sharper answer is “moment of inertia,” not plain inertia. If the clues give a formula or a unit like kilograms, the answer is probably “mass.” Save “inertia” for clues about Newton’s First Law, reference frames, and the general tendency to resist changes in motion.
trap.line: Real answer line: Inertia (accept inertial); a related answer line, “moment of inertia,” explicitly does not accept or prompt on bare “inertia.”
